title: Saina Nehwal Says India Must Top Medals Tally to Be Called a Sporting Nation
excerpt: The Olympic bronze medallist and former world No. 1 called for better financial backing, sports psychologists, and systemic support for athletes beyond cricket during a college event in Mumbai.
body:
• Saina Nehwal said India must feature among the top nations in medals tallies to truly call itself a "sporting nation," amid the country's push to host global competitions including the Olympics.
  • The retired badminton champion highlighted a growing change in women's sports, particularly athletes from Haryana excelling in wrestling, boxing, and badminton.
  • Nehwal called for financial security systems similar to cricket for athletes in other sports, including salary structures and job guarantees.
  • She emphasized the need for more sports psychologists and mental trainers, saying out of 10 athletes, only 2-3 can perform at their best without such support.

Former world No. 1 shuttler and Olympic bronze medallist Saina Nehwal has said that India needs to feature among the top nations in medals tallies before it can genuinely call itself a "sporting nation." Speaking at Malhar, an inter-collegiate festival hosted by St Xavier's College in Mumbai, Nehwal addressed the gap between India's ambitions to host global sporting events and its actual competitive output, NDTV Sports reported.

"We are trying (to host) Olympics or big tournaments but I think one thing we have to make sure is that we are in top of the medal tally as well and that is when we can call ourselves a sporting nation," Nehwal said.

Women's Sports: Progress and Gaps

Nehwal, who retired from professional badminton in January 2026 after a two-decade career, observed that female sportspersons in India have increasingly realized their potential. "Somewhere women are realizing that we are capable, we can do well," she said, according to NDTV Sports.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=keucElApbfE

She pointed to visible progress over the past 15-20 years, particularly among women athletes from Haryana. "I keep seeing that, especially lot of girls from Haryana, they are doing extremely well in sports and wrestling, boxing, badminton is coming up," Nehwal said. "I just want it to happen throughout the country so that we can be called as sporting nation in the future."

The Money Problem

Nehwal was blunt about the financial challenges facing athletes outside cricket. She said that without reaching the top 15 or top 20 in world rankings, athletes struggle to secure sponsorships or adequate funding.

"It's not like cricket… still you have to improve a lot more but if you are consistent, if you are performing well, of course you will get all kind of sponsorships but not many players are like so talented."

— Saina Nehwal, Olympic bronze medallist

"Unless we improve the promotions, marketing, sponsorships from really early age, that is when I think we can get many more players," she added, per NDTV Sports.

The former champion advocated for financial security systems comparable to cricket — salary structures and job guarantees that allow athletes to treat their sport as a full-time profession. "At least when you play best in the world, you have that salary system, you have that job system and then you can take it as your profession. But other sports still are lacking behind it and that's why many of them just lose the interest," Nehwal said.

Mental Health and Coaching Infrastructure

Beyond money, Nehwal highlighted a critical gap in India's sporting infrastructure: the lack of sports psychologists and mental health professionals. "That is the problem in most of the sports that you don't have psychologists, you don't have proper trainers and proper physios," she said.

She said the situation has improved in the last 5-6 years but remains insufficient. "We need lot of psychologists, lot of mental trainers in our sports so that out of 10, at least six of them can perform. Otherwise, from your own will, from your own fighting attitude, there are only 2-3 people who can do well," Nehwal said, according to NDTV Sports.

A Legacy That Reshaped Indian Badminton

Nehwal's career spanned 24 international titles, including ten Superseries victories, an Olympic bronze medal at London 2012, two Commonwealth Games singles golds (2010 and 2018), and a World Championships silver medal in 2015. She was the first Indian badminton player to win an Olympic medal and the first Indian woman to reach the BWF World Championships final. In 2015, she became only the second Indian player — after Prakash Padukone — to attain the world No. 1 ranking. She was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2016.
